meta.title: Distributed Rate Limiter
meta.summary: Enforce per-API-key limits consistently across many gateway instances with an atomic token bucket in Redis.

functional: Limit each API key to N requests per second, with short bursts allowed
Return 429 with Retry-After when over the limit
Limits differ by plan and can change without a deploy
nonFunctional: Limits hold across all gateway instances combined
If the limiter itself fails, the API keeps serving (fail open)

scale.label: Gateways
scale.value: 75 instances at ~20k requests/s each: 50 carry the peak, the rest cover a lost zone

scale.label: API keys
scale.value: 5M, each a small hash in Redis while active

slos.name: Limiter overhead
slos.sli: Limit decisions made within the threshold, divided by all decisions, timed inside the gateway

slos.name: API availability with the limiter
slos.sli: Requests answered without a 5xx (429s count as good), divided by all requests, at the gateways, even when the limiter is degraded

slos.name: Limit accuracy
slos.sli: Keys that hit their limit and were admitted within 5% of their configured rate, divided by all keys that hit their limit, from per-key decision counts sampled each minute

alerts.when: API errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: The limiter must never be the reason the API is down.

alerts.when: API errors burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak that would use up the month's budget in ten days.

alerts.when: Slow limit decisions burning the latency budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Every API request pays this latency.

alerts.when: Counter store p99 above 2 ms for 10 minutes
alerts.why: The limiter adds that latency to every request.

alerts.when: Fail-open decisions above zero for 5 minutes
alerts.why: Limits are not being enforced. Page if it lasts 15 minutes.

alerts.when: Rejection ratio for one key above 50% for 10 minutes
alerts.why: An abusive client, or a plan limit set too low for what they need.

alerts.when: Gateways running a limits table older than 5 minutes
alerts.why: Plan changes and overrides are not taking effect.

alerts.when: Counter Store memory above 80%, any evictions, or one shard's CPU above 70% while the others are below 40%
alerts.why: Evictions reset buckets to full allowances; one busy shard means a hot key that needs the batching approach.

signals.name: Fail-open count
signals.why: Counts requests let through because the counter store was unreachable.

signals.name: Latency and evictions
signals.why: An evicted bucket resets a key to a full allowance.

signals.name: Allowed against rejected, by plan
signals.why: Shows whether limits match how customers really use the API.

signals.name: Script calls per shard
signals.why: Shows hot keys and how close each shard is to its limit.

signals.name: Circuit breaker state
signals.why: Open means every decision on that gateway is local and approximate.

debug.symptom: Customers get 429 responses they should not
steps: Check the limit the gateway has for that key: is the config table fresh?
Look at that key's decisions over time: a burst or sustained traffic?
Check counter store evictions and failovers: lost state changes the allowance.
The script reads Redis TIME, so gateway clock drift is not the cause.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the API hostname at the load balancer

nodes.label: Network Load Balancer
nodes.description: Layer 4 in front of the gateways; Envoy does all HTTP-level work

nodes.label: Gateway + Limiter
nodes.description: Envoy fleet in private subnets; rate-limit middleware in every instance, plus L7 filtering (the NLB cannot carry a WAF)

nodes.label: Counter Store
nodes.description: Token buckets in a Redis cluster sharded by API key (about 10 shards plus headroom), each shard primary + replica in different zones

nodes.label: Limits Config
nodes.description: plan → rate, burst; per-key overrides; hashed API keys. Reached through a VPC endpoint

flows.title: Allowed request
flows.summary: One atomic round trip to Redis decides, then the request continues to the backend.

steps.label: resolve api.example.com
steps.detail: A network load balancer has fixed IP addresses, which customers can allowlist in their firewalls. DNS answers with them and clients cache the result.

steps.label: any gateway
steps.detail: Requests from one key land on many gateways, which is why the count must be shared and not kept in local memory. The NLB health-checks every Envoy instance and stops sending to failed ones.

steps.label: auth key_abc, limit (cached)
steps.detail: Envoy checks the key against the hashed keys and plan limits it caches in memory, refreshed in the background, so config is not on the hot path. A key it has never seen gets the free plan's limit until the next refresh. Envoy also runs the L7 filters a WAF would (request size, header and path rules), since an NLB cannot host one.

steps.label: EVALSHA token_bucket
steps.detail: A Lua script runs atomically inside Redis: refill tokens for the time elapsed, then take one. It reads the clock with Redis TIME, so gateway clock skew cannot add tokens, and it sets an expiry so idle keys vanish once their bucket would be full again.
steps.payload:
-- KEYS[1] = tb:key_abc   ARGV = rate per s, burst
local rate, burst = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2])
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] + t[2] / 1e6
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = math.min(burst, (tonumber(b[1]) or burst) + (now - (tonumber(b[2]) or now)) * rate)
local ok = tokens >= 1
if ok then tokens = tokens - 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(burst / rate * 1000))
return { ok and 1 or 0, tostring(tokens), tostring((1 - tokens) / rate) }  -- allowed, left, wait s

steps.label: forward
steps.detail: Envoy balances across the backend instances itself (least requests, active health checks, outlier ejection), so no extra load balancer sits here. It starts the trace and adds the key's id for the backend.
steps.payload:
GET /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
traceparent: 00-9c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0a1b2c3d4e5f-1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b-01
X-Api-Key-Id: key_abc
X-RateLimit-Plan: pro

flows.title: Throttled request
flows.summary: The bucket is empty: reject at the edge without touching the backend.

steps.label: EVALSHA token_bucket
steps.detail: The same script; the bucket is empty, so it returns how long until one token refills.

steps.label: 429 Too Many Requests
steps.detail: The backend never sees the request. Retry-After is in whole seconds, so 0.4 s rounds up to 1.

steps.label: 429, retry after 1 s
steps.detail: Well-behaved clients back off with jitter.

flows.title: Counter store down (fail open)
flows.summary: A limiter outage must not become an API outage.

steps.label: EVALSHA token_bucket
steps.detail: The call has a 5 ms timeout.

steps.label: timeout: breaker opens, local limit
steps.detail: Fail open with a coarse local limit (key limit ÷ number of gateways). After a few timeouts a circuit breaker stops calling Redis for a few seconds, so requests do not each wait 5 ms while it is down. Briefly over-admitting is better than rejecting all traffic.

flows.title: Limits refresh
flows.summary: Background refresh keeps plan changes live without a deploy.

steps.label: GET limits changed since t
steps.detail: Every ~30 s each gateway reads changes from an index on updated_at, through a VPC endpoint. A customer upgrade takes effect within a minute; 75 gateways polling is trivial load.

notes.text: Algorithms: fixed window (simple, bursty at window edges), sliding log (exact, memory-heavy), sliding window counter (good approximation), token bucket (allows controlled bursts). Token bucket is the usual pick for APIs.

Shard Redis by API key so each key's bucket lives on one shard. A shard runs on the order of 100k small scripts a second, so 1M/s needs about 10 shards plus headroom; each shard has a replica in another zone. A single very hot key still lands on one shard (see the hybrid note).

The script reads Redis TIME, so gateway clock skew does not matter. Replication is asynchronous, so a replica promoted after failover may have slightly old counts, and an evicted bucket starts full: both briefly over-admit, which is acceptable for rate limiting.
Hybrid for very hot keys: each gateway takes tokens from Redis in small batches and spends them locally, cutting Redis calls by 10× at a small cost in precision.
A network (L4) load balancer is enough here because the gateways already parse HTTP. It adds less latency, handles huge connection counts and can expose static IPs that customers allowlist.
Static IPs from the network load balancer let enterprise customers allowlist the API. Plan any IP change carefully: they cache and firewall these addresses.

There is no WAF component: AWS WAF cannot attach to a network load balancer. DDoS protection comes from Shield Advanced on the NLB (or Cloud Armor network edge policies on GCP), and L7 rules run in Envoy. Teams that need managed WAF rule sets put CloudFront or an ALB with AWS WAF in front, giving up the static IPs.

questions.q: Token bucket, fixed window or sliding window: which would you choose and why?
questions.a: A token bucket allows short bursts up to a cap while enforcing an average rate, and needs only a count and a timestamp per key. Fixed windows are simpler but let a client send double the limit across a window boundary. A sliding window is the most accurate and costs more memory or computation.

questions.q: Many gateway instances update the same client's counter. How do you avoid race conditions?
questions.a: Do the check-and-decrement as one atomic operation in the counter store, for example a Lua script or an atomic increment with expiry in Redis. Reading the value and writing it back in two steps lets concurrent requests both pass. Each request costs one round trip to the store.

questions.q: The counter store goes down. Do you block all traffic or let everything through?
questions.a: Usually fail open: let requests through with a local, per-instance approximate limit, and trip a circuit breaker so requests stop waiting on the dead store. Rejecting everything turns a limiter outage into a full outage. Fail closed only for limits that protect money or security, such as login attempts. Alert either way.

questions.q: How do you keep the limiter from adding noticeable latency to every request?
questions.a: Keep the counter store close (same zone) and in memory, with one atomic call per request. For very high rates, keep local counters in each gateway and sync with the shared store in batches, accepting a small overshoot. Never call the store more than once per request.

questions.q: How do limits change per customer plan without a deploy?
questions.a: Store limits in a config store keyed by plan or customer, and have gateways cache them and refresh periodically or on a change event. Validate changes and roll them out gradually, since a bad limit can block every customer at once.

questions.q: What should a throttled client receive?
questions.a: Return HTTP 429 with headers that say the limit, how many requests remain and when to retry (Retry-After). Good clients back off using them. Return the headers on successful responses too, so clients can slow down before they hit the limit.
